item.title: A critical flaw in PHP, ‘backbone of the web’, has cyber experts scrambling for a fix
item.description: The incident shows that vulnerabilities will recur as long as the world treats open-source foundational tools charity rather than critical security investment.
item.content:encoded:
Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline.

The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.

The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time.

What is PHP?

PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes.

The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites.

item.title: Opinion: India should welcome Musk’s Starlink – but ensure that it holds the switch
item.description: Satellite internet can connect the millions still offline. The question is not whether it comes but who controls it when it matters.
item.content:encoded:
On October 7, businessman Elon Musk took to X to accuse unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking the entry into India of Starlink, his service that uses a network of low-orbitting satellites to deliver high-speed broadband internet. Musk claimed that this was a “crime against the people of India”.

However, the Indian government said that Musk’s claim was “baseless and misconceived”. It said all three licensed operators of satellite internet (satcom) services in India – Elon Musk’s Starlink, Reliance Jio’s Jio Satcom and the Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb – are at broadly the same stage of the regulatory approval process, each awaiting security clearance before spectrum is assigned.

The spat makes for good theatre. But it frames the wrong question. The issue is not whether Starlink should come to India. It is on whose terms and who will hold the switch when it matters.

Digital divide

India had nearly 1.09 billion internet subscriptions at the end of March, according to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India. That hides a divide. Cities have about 127 subscriptions per 100 people but rural India has about 48.

By the estimates of the Internet and Mobile Association of India industry group, roughly 38% of Indians – nearly 58 crore people – are still not active internet users.

item.title: Singer Diljit Dosanjh gets police clearance for Delhi concert
item.description: ‘Permission for the event had been temporarily withheld, not cancelled, and the two should not be confused,’ said ticketing platform BookMyShow.
item.content:encoded:
The Delhi Police has granted permission for singer Diljit Dosanjh’s concert at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on October 30, IANS quoted the event’s ticketing partner BookMyShow as saying on Friday.

This came a day after the police denied clearance for the event because of threat-related inputs and security requirements during the festive season.

The Hindu festival of Diwali will be celebrated on November 8.

On Friday, BookMyShow clarified that any media reports claiming that the concert had been cancelled were inaccurate.

“Permission for the event had been temporarily withheld, not cancelled, and the two should not be confused,” IANS quoted the platform as saying.

It added that the police had asked the concert’s organisers and BookMyShow to ensure additional safety and traffic management measures.

“BookMyShow Live had a cordial meeting with Delhi Police, presented a detailed plan and have assured Delhi Police of full compliance with all security/traffic requirements,” said the ticketing platform.

It added: “On that basis, permission for the event has been reconsidered and issued.”

After Delhi, Dosanjh is scheduled to perform in Indore, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Lucknow and Chandigarh in November and December as part of his Aura India Tour.

item.title: From a new compilation of tales from mythology and folklore: Vasishtha looks for a place to meditate
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Blue Lotus: Myths and Folk Tales of India’, by Meena Arora Nayak.
item.content:encoded:
Seeking to detach himself from the world, Rishi Vasishtha looked for a place where he could meditate in seclusion – a place without the distractions of the city, forest, sky, ocean, clouds, creatures, gods, or souls. He found a spot in space that was so far away from earth that even the natural elements could not reach it. In that empty place, he imagined a small hermitage and made it inaccessible to the rest of the world. Then he sat down in it in the lotus posture, and quietening his mind, went into samadhi for a hundred years.

On awakening, when he willed his consciousness to return, he heard a sigh. In this place of his imagination, which was so far away in empty space, where not even air could intrude, he wondered where that sound was coming from, and from whom. So he went back into the infinite consciousness of his mind and began searching. In his mind were order and disorder and countless universes in different stages of creation and destruction. item.title: SBI says it informed customers after details of nearly 3,900 account holders leaked in cyberattack
item.description: Around 3.75 lakh customer records were released on the dark web, of which 3,897 contained personally identifiable information.
item.content:encoded:
The State Bank of India on Friday said it had individually informed customers whose personal data was leaked on the dark web following a cyberattack, using email or WhatsApp.

The cyberattack on Wednesday had led to the leak of about 3.75 lakh customer records on the dark web, of which 3,897 contained personally identifiable information.

The bank’s statement came after digital rights organisation Internet Freedom Foundation flagged that SBI had informed stock exchanges about the data leak but had not notified affected customers.

In its statement on Friday, the SBI said that customers’ account balances and funds were safe. “Customers are advised to follow safe digital banking practices, never share their OTP, PIN or password with anyone, and remain vigilant against suspicious calls, messages and emails,” it added.

In July, customer data and internal documents from state-run Bank of Baroda were also leaked on the dark web, Reuters reported.

The Reserve Bank of India has repeatedly warned lenders about cybersecurity risks that could affect financial stability.

item.title: Uttar Pradesh: ‘Irregularities’ found in over 10,000 entries to Pilibhit electoral rolls

Rinwa also announced that legal action will be taken against the current and former electoral registration officers in the constituency, while the services of a computer assistant at the Voter Registration Centre of Pilibhit will be terminated.

The action was taken after an investigation by the Pilibhit district election officer showed that the computer assistant had entered 13,779 Form 8 applications.

Form 8 is meant for shifting residence and correcting details in an existing electoral roll.

“No forms or records related to any of these entries were found available in the office,” said the chief election officer.

He added that of the total, 10,470 forms for “corrections” were approved. Irregularities were found in all of them, said Rinwa.

item.title: ‘Gajab Raat’ review: Manoj Bajpayee fires up a thriller that runs out of steam
item.description: Ritesh Shah’s Hindi thriller, co-written with Neeraj Pandey, is out on Netflix.
item.content:encoded:
In 2023, Manoj Bajpayee headlined the aptly titled film Sirf Ek Bandaa Kaafi Hai, playing a lawyer who refuses to come under pressure for representing a rape survivor. All it takes is one unwavering man – Bajpayee has come to embody this dogged, obdurate and cussed person, who acts as he pleases and moves sidewinder-like towards justice. Gajab Raat needs exactly such a person.

Ritesh Shah’s Hindi film, co-written with and produced by Neeraj Pandey, stars Bajpayee as Ajay, a lowly Delhi Police inspector who finds himself in charge of a knotty case. A grievously injured young woman has been found lying on a street in Delhi. Her identity is a mystery.

Several important people want to get to her, including social worker Neha (Shraddha Das), the Central Bureau of Investigation’s Madhok (Akshay Oberoi) and the National Investigation Agency’s Karan (Saqib Saleem). They have to get past Ajay, who creates a Great Wall-like barrier with not entirely altruistic motives.

Ajay has a reputation for selling out to the highest bidder. The latest case will prove whether Ajay is a sell-out or a hero.

The cast includes Rajiv Gupta as Ajay’s senior officer, Kiku Sharda as a hotel owner and Nushrratt Bharuccha as one of Ajay’s special friends.

item.title: Brand story: How entrepreneur MP Ramachandran made Ujala fabric whitener a laundry bestseller
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Brief Case: How Brands Create Desire, Trust and Culture’, by Sanjay Arora.
item.content:encoded:
Most problems that change the world don’t look like problems at all.

They look like mild inconveniences, the kind of thing most people shrug off and live with.

MP Ramachandran couldn’t shrug it off. He was obsessed with white clothes, wore only white shirts, washed them himself and was perpetually dissatisfied with the result. The whites faded, they yellowed, they looked like they’d given up. And every fabric whitener on the market made the problem worse rather than better.

Most people would have bought a different shirt.

Ramachandran built a company.


MP Ramachandran was not a typical entrepreneur. He was an accountant working in Mumbai who wore only white. His biggest frustration was that whites never stayed that way, they faded quickly, stains showed more easily and they looked old and ragged faster than coloured clothes.

That frustration became the catalyst.

Robin Blue was the dominant player in fabric whiteners at the time. But the problem with these powders was the process: consumers had to manually dissolve the powder, strain it through cloth and hope it didn’t leave blue patches on the fabric. Messy, unreliable and it still didn’t deliver the whiteness it promised.

item.title: FDA suspends licences of 8 Mumbai eateries, seizes 38 tonnes of food stock in Maharashtra
item.description: The establishments whose permits were held include You Mee in Ghatkopar and a Domino’s Pizza outlet in Bhandup.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration suspended the licences of eight eateries in Mumbai and seized nearly 38 tonnes of food stock worth Rs 54.6 lakh across the state during inspections on Wednesday and Thursday.

The inspections uncovered violations, including unhygienic kitchens and drainage systems, rusted racks and utensils, incomplete temperature records, workers without medical certificates and the use of unauthorised food colours in sweets.

The establishments whose licences were suspended in Mumbai are SK Bakery in Mazgaon, Nekzad Restaurant in Grant Road, Foodies Multi Cuisine in Bandra, Arabian Luqma in Jogeshwari and Delhi Zaika in Kurla. The list also includes You Mee in Ghatkopar, a Domino’s Pizza outlet in Bhandup and Bikkgane Biryani in Govandi-Chembur.

The Food and Drug Administration said that the licences had been suspended with immediate effect. However, it did not specify which violations were found at each establishment.

As for the seizures, the largest was reported in Navi Mumbai, where officials confiscated 33,286 kg of kidney beans and other pulses worth about Rs 50 lakh from RDC Agro Ventures in the Shirwane area of Nerul.

The department said that the products were suspected to be substandard and incorrectly labelled.

item.title: ‘Udta Teer’ review: Cartoonish spy comedy is low in general intelligence
item.description: Ayushmann Khurrana leads Akash A Kaushik’s film.
item.content:encoded:
For all those wondering whether there is anything left to say about spies on lengthy missions in hostile territory after Dhurandhar, here is Udta Teer. In Akash A Kaushik’s Hindi-language comedy, the situation is reversed: a Pakistani agent has worked his way up to the top of India’s counter-terrorism unit.

Bilal (Ayushmann Khurrana), who is passing himself off as Vikrant, is not only his agency’s top operative but also a family man – his wife Yamini (Sara Ali Khan) is in the Defence ministry. When Bilal’s boss Burman (Rahul Bose) suspects that there is a mole in his office, he asks Bilal to investigate. Such is the trust that Bilal commands.

Alas, Bilal is scheming away in the shadows along with a couple of other undercover Pakistanis. Bilal arranges the escape of Pakistani terrorist Maqsood (Mukul Dev) but then loses his memory.

Bilal wakes up as Vikrant, confused about which country he is supposed to protect. Bilal is now a true-blue Indian patriot, who prays in a Hindu temple with gusto and goes after Maqsood with a vengeance.

item.title: Review: ‘Magazine’ is at a loose end, like its Gen Z hero
item.description: Shubham Shevade’s Marathi film, starring Raghav Vartak, is out in cinemas.
item.content:encoded:
Velu is bored, listless and confused about his future. The affluent and coddled young man fits some stereotypes about Gen Z, especially when he grandly “resigns” from a magazine published by his father after being scoffed at for wanting to explore “conflict”.

In search of inspiration and direction, Velu (Raghav Vartak) takes off for his father’s sugarcane farm in his ancestral village of Dattawad. Velu’s roseate memories of Dattawad are somewhat at odds with its present. Nothing much has changed here, Velu marvels – something his childhood friends Shripadh (Sudarshan Deshmukh) and Pushkar (Nilesh Mane) do not entirely agree with.

Magazine, which is out in cinemas, wants to pursue a back-to-roots story that is complicated by reality. Shubham Sanjay Shevade’s Marathi-language drama, co-written with Prateek Handore, is big on flashbacks, montages and scenes built around unstructured conversations as Velu tries to find his footing.

Velu flirts with farming – the village needs “at least one Brahmin” farmer, a character says – and tries to understand the gnomic villager (Kishor Kadam). Like Velu, the film thrashes about too, unsure of where it intends to go next.

item.title: Review: ‘Doosra’ tries to force-fit two incompatible ideas
item.description: Abhinay Deo’s film is a hybrid between documentary and fiction, with a starring role for Sourav Ganguly.
item.content:encoded:
Abhinay Deo’s Doosra refers to, all at once, the delivery style in cricket, the endeavour of the story’s heroine to seek an alternative to her miserable life and the film’s hybrid form. Doosra is part-documentary and part-fictional feature, in which former Indian captain Sourav Ganguly fires the imagination of a cricket-loving woman in a small town.

The story unfolds between 1991 and 2002. Tara (Plabita Borthakur) belongs to a conservative family in which women are expected to know their place. When Tara speaks up, she is slapped by her strict father (Ankur Vikal). Elsewhere, the Indian cricket team is getting beaten up too, as is the country itself.

In unsure times, amidst a balance of payments crisis and a cricket betting scandal, Sourav Ganguly stands for much-needed chutzpah, his reputation for arrogance and his refusal to take orders just what the country’s battered image needs, according to Doosra. The story, by Rohan Sajdeh and Agnello Dias, imagines Ganguly as the spearhead of newfound assertion, most vividly expressed in the cricketer’s notorious shirtless celebration of India’s victory over England at the Lord’s Cricket Ground in the NatWest Series in 2002.

item.title: Review: ‘Tu Hai Meri Kiran’ puts a twist on stalking
item.description: Karan Rawal’s thriller stars Sonakshi Sinha, Zaheer Iqbal and Ankit Gupta.
item.content:encoded:
Tu Hai Meri Kiran gets its title from the song of the same name in Darr (1993), about a deranged man who harasses the woman with whom he is obsessed. Karan Rawal’s film, which is out in cinemas, gives stalking an intriguing, and absorbing, twist.

Kiran (Sonakshi Sinha) finds an old flip phone in her house in Mussoorie that connects her to Samar (Zaheer Iqbal). Kiran is a writer struggling to complete her second novel, and is married to Riyaan (Ankit Gupta). Samar, troubled and in trouble for his noxious behaviour, will prove to be a handful for Kiran.

Rawal’s screenplay, which borrows its major idea from a Korean show, is laden with suspense. The least twisty aspect of Tu Hai Meri Kiran is that stalking behaviour, which is condoned by the euphemism “one-sided love”, has frightening staying power. This idea gives a tinge of horror to Karan Rawal’s screenplay, despite strenuous efforts to humanise Samar and give him a tear-jerking back story.

Rawal admirably maintains an air of tension across 125 minutes. Some willing suspension of disbelief is necessary to go along with the film’s conceit. item.title: Why India needs citizen-centric governance for everyday democracy
item.description: Significant effort is required to extract even basic accountability from the state.
item.content:encoded:
In recent months, young Indians have felt compelled to petition, protest, run aggressive social media campaigns and push back against the government’s business-as-usual approach to irregularities in the manner in which electoral lists are being revised and in the way examinations are being conducted.

These protests reflect a wider frustration with the lack of avenues for citizens to engage with and hold accountable the governments and representatives they elect across levels.

Between the five-year election cycles, citizens have few systemic avenues to engage with their elected leaders and governments, contribute to decision-making, track commitments and projects or seek remedial action.

When the state fails to offer meaningful platforms for engagement and accountability, people are left with no options but to resort to protests on matters as basic as access to drinking water, quality education, health care or pothole-free roads or obstacle-free footpaths or fair examinations and recruitment to government services.

In his Grammar of Anarchy speech on the eve of the adoption of the Constitution in 1949, BR Ambedkar argued for abandoning the method of civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha since constitutional methods (including legal means of enforcing civil rights, obtaining services, legislating new laws, or seeking accountability from the government through courts and tribunals) were now available.

After escaping a particularly frenetic shootout, the narrator of Chaar Yaar says, “This was like a movie... not the KJo kind but the RGV kind.”

The long shadow of Ram Gopal Varma, the chief purveyor of the gangster genre, looms over Chaar Yaar, directed by Vinay Waikul. One of the creators of the Prime Video show is underworld expert S Hussain Zaidi, the others being Waikul, Sambit Mishra and Saurabh Sawant. There are several allusions to Varma’s Satya, which was released a few years before the 2001 setting of the series.

The four friends are a disparate lot. The brain is Jay (Prayrak Mehta), also the narrator, whose flip tone makes light of the upheavals upending their middle class existence. item.title: A new book shows how modern education became the first step to freedom for womxn in British India
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Forgotten Feminisms: A Subversive Retelling of Indian Womxn’s Resistance’, by Sindhu Rajasekaran.
item.content:encoded:
Parvati Nawar, a fish-seller from a presidency town, wrote a letter to the government of the British Raj in 1883 seeking protection from the police. She complained that the police were oppressing vendors at the local market.

Not only is it awe-inspiring that she stood up to the might of authority, but that she wrote her letter in a format colonial authorities couldn’t ignore or erase from their archives. Although we do not know whether the government intervened to end her grievance, the letter is illustrative of the sort of social consciousness that was prevalent at the time in British India.

The importance of modern education cannot be stated more here. While caste and class still determined one’s access to education across the subcontinent, it was slowly democratised in presidency towns thanks to subaltern(ised) social reform movements that worked in tandem with colonial policy. Meanwhile, in parts of India where missionary education and evangelisation were concomitant, entire tribes converted to Christianity, and with it came modern literacy.

Thomas Miranda (Hridansh Parekh) has two pressing concerns: where do babies come from, and how can he get a baby brother? When he was six, he wanted a zoo; now at seven, he is convinced that he needs a sibling. His attempt to find answers lead him to a priest, his kindly neighbour Mrs Braganza (Mahabanoo Mody-Kotwal) and conversations with his two friends: Nigel, who has an insatiable appetite, and Murthy, a science enthusiast.

Thomas’s parents Desmond (Gulshan Devaiah) and Jessie (Rasika Dugal) run a bakery, but business is slow. Jessie teaches piano, but dwindling interest among children in learning music threatens her livelihood. Desmond and Jessie’s disagreements are shaped by everyday pressures, though Thomas, naturally, sees things in much simpler terms.

item.title: What is the Socratic method? Could it be used to test students in the age of AI?
item.description: Classrooms should encourage and asses dialogue as opposed to purely descriptive assessments to assist a student’s learning.
item.content:encoded:
Most students now use AI in their tertiary studies. AI can also, under certain conditions, answer at least 65% of questions correctly in STEM subjects.

In the humanities, where the whole aim is critical and creative reflection, educators face a thorny question. How do you develop and measure thinking of the kind that a machine could not genuinely imitate?

AI has proven it can answer questions well. But can it ask questions? And can it ask the right questions?

This is the philosophical method at the heart of the work of the Ancient Greek philosopher, Plato. His Socratic method of teaching is, perhaps, the mode of thinking we need to emulate in our teaching and learning today.

The great questions

Plato wrote dialogues: texts that read (in nearly every case) like a conversation between Socrates (Plato’s teacher) and a partner drawn into conversation by Socrates after claiming to know something about living a good and virtuous life.

There is a dialogue for all the great philosophical questions: what justice is; what courage or love really requires; what makes a good friend; and even how we acquire knowledge.

item.title: Rejoinder: Use of Kafka’s cockroach metaphor for Dalit identity undermines anti-caste politics
item.description: The legacy of Dalit politics is resistance and defying dehumanisation.
item.content:encoded:
In his article “Being a Dalit, being a cockroach: A self-reflective note on Kafka’s ‘Metamorphosis’”, Bhimraj M, a scholar at University of Oxford, uses an autobiographical lens and diagnoses his dalitness as a Kafkaesque condition. He compares his place in the caste society to that of Franz Kafka’s cockroach character Gregor Samsa.

As Dalit scholar-activists from Delhi University and Jawaharlal Nehru University we find this metaphor inappropriate, misleading and potentially regressive. Dalit consciousness, we argue, is fundamentally political, not existential and it requires analogies that foreground active resistance.

Bhimraj is admittedly comfortable in his “familiar” cockroach-ness, and detests being humanised. Yet, he yearns for and, eventually, resolves to seek a humanness for himself. “How am I supposed to feel when my fellow Dalit students are forced to clean bathrooms in schools, humiliated as ‘quotawallas’ or even driven to suicide in colleges?” he asks.

Enraged, we say! Such has been the approach of Dalit movement from Phule to Ambedkar and Kanshiram. The Dalit Panther movement of the 1970s sought to transform indignation into collective resistance, with “Panther” symbolising strength and defiance against oppression.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Cashless Nation: How UPI Changed Everything’, by Santanu Paul and B Sambamurthy.
item.content:encoded:
UPI is a major agent of transformation, but seen through the prism of geography, prosperity and gender, it is the story of an uneven revolution. The adoption gap between rich and poor states, urban and rural regions, as well as men and women, remains substantial. Despite UPI’s relentless march across the length and breadth of the country, there are large swathes of the economy where cash still reigns supreme.

A handful of prosperous states serve as torchbearers for the revolution. Between April and June 2025, Maharashtra led with over 6 billion UPI transactions, nearly twice that of Karnataka, which came in shy of 4 billion. Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu followed. Four of these states are more industrialised and more prosperous. The exception is Uttar Pradesh, but it is a huge state in terms of population, so it records high transaction volumes in absolute terms. A look at state-wise per capita UPI usage further reveals that residents of richer states average about 13 UPI transactions per month. item.title: From taboo subject, menopause is now a big business opportunity
item.description: Does it genuinely meet women’s needs, or does it help create a new market?

Long relegated to the private sphere, Menopause is now the focus of unprecedented attention both in the media and commercially with a market value of 535 billion euros ($600 billion). The amount of books, podcasts, documentaries, digital applications, food supplements and coaching programs is multiplying to support women in this stage of life. What was once a taboo subject has become a booming economic sector.

This evolution constitutes an important step forward: people are talking more about menopause, it is better understood and is gradually being recognised as a public health issue. But this visibility is also accompanied by bold marketing. As the topic enters the public arena, it also becomes a niche market opportunity.

This transformation raises a question at the heart of the analysis in All Change! Marketing and Consuming the Menopause Transition: does it genuinely meet women’s needs, or does it help create a new market built on their concerns, symptoms and desire for wellbeing?

Political cartoonist Satish Acharya’s Instagram account was restricted in India for the second time in three weeks on Tuesday.

A message displayed by the Meta-owned platform when users try to access the account says: “We temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules.”

“Saheb, people have elected you to bring achche din,” he wrote referring to the government. “You are wasting your term in blocking Instagram accounts!”

He added: “Who is so scared of cartoon!”

Acharya’s Instagram account had been restricted in India on September 28 after the platform received a legal request from the government under the 2021 Information Technology Rules. item.title: When mangrove restoration projects become big business
item.description: It has become a new kind of market. But it also distributes what it generates along a chain of intermediaries, with little reaching local communities.
item.content:encoded:
On Pakistan’s Indus delta coast, a 350,000-hectare mangrove project is turning a growing forest into something that can be sold to companies thousands of miles away: carbon credits.

Carbon credits allow companies to pay for projects that store carbon or prevent further emissions, with each credit equalling a certain amount of carbon. Restoring mangroves can generate credits as a healthy, growing forest absorbs and stores carbon. It’s part of a thriving billion dollar industry.

But that forest was already worth something to the thousands of people living there. It protects 60 villages from storms, provides nursery habitat for fish and is a source of wood, honey and thatch.

The difference points to a bigger problem. A mangrove has at least two kinds of value: the value that can be packaged and sold to a (wealthy) distant buyer, and the value that is experienced locally but is much harder to monetise. Only the first has a market built around it.

This gap will be under the spotlight at the upcoming UN climate summit Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, this November. item.title: India at growing risk of infectious diseases due to climate change effects
item.description: Excess rainfall allows bacteria and viruses to thrive and spread while drought-like conditions can intensify transmission and hygiene dangers.
item.content:encoded:
When extreme weather events occur, the damage is usually measured in collapsed buildings, damaged roads and flooded homes. But the aftermath also brings a less visible threat.

Heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall and flash floods, in combination or alone, also reshape the ecology of diseases. They can affect how long pathogens survive, change the distribution of disease-carrying insects and bring people, animals and pathogens into closer contact, increasing the risk of outbreaks in new places at unexpected times.

Form 6 is meant for first-time voter registration.

The court made the observation while closing a petition filed by two persons whose names were deleted from the draft electoral roll in Delhi after they could not complete the SIR enumeration process following a change of residence.

The petitioners had challenged the poll panel’s direction requiring existing electors who were left out during the SIR to seek fresh inclusion through Form 6, rather than use Form 8 to correct or shift their existing electoral entries.

Form 8 is meant for shifting residence and correcting details in an existing electoral roll.

They sought to have their names restored to the electoral roll and moved to the constituency where they now lived.

The poll panel told the court that the petitioners could seek the restoration of their names by submitting Form 6.
